genre/vroege-synthesizerscores-moog-berl.text: In 1971, Wendy Carlos used a Moog synthesizer for A Clockwork Orange, with electronic versions of Beethoven and Purcell and pieces of her own. After that, the synthesizer became a fully fledged film instrument. The Berlin group Tangerine Dream, with sequencers that play endless, pulsing patterns, made the music for William Friedkin's Sorcerer (1977). The Greek composer Vangelis won an Oscar for Chariots of Fire (1981), with synthesizer and piano. In Blade Runner (1982), he created a melancholy, nocturnal cityscape with the Yamaha CS-80. Carlos returned with Tron (1982), in which orchestra and synthesizer go together. In this way, electronic music gained a permanent place in Hollywood.
genre/vroege-synthesizerscores-moog-berl.listen: Notice the pulsing sequencer patterns and the difference between synthesizers that imitate an orchestra and sounds that are only possible electronically.

genre/wagner-en-het-muziekdrama.text: Richard Wagner no longer wanted opera made up of separate numbers, but a continuous music drama in which music, text and stage form a single whole. Characters and ideas were given a recognisable motif of their own, the leitmotif, with which the orchestra helps tell the story. In Tristan und Isolde (1865), Wagner postpones the resolution of his dissonant chords for hours. In 1876, his own festival theatre opened in Bayreuth with the complete Ring des Nibelungen.
genre/wagner-en-het-muziekdrama.listen: Hear how, in the prelude to Tristan und Isolde, every phrase longs for a point of rest that keeps failing to arrive.

genre/weense-klassiek.text: In the second half of the eighteenth century, Vienna became the centre of a clear, balanced style. Joseph Haydn, in the service of the Esterházy family, developed the symphony and the string quartet; Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart came to Vienna in 1781 and Ludwig van Beethoven in 1792. They built their pieces in sonata form: two contrasting themes are presented, developed and return. Beethoven stretched that form to the stormy Fifth Symphony of 1808.
genre/weense-klassiek.listen: Hear how the violins keep repeating and spinning out the short, sighing motif of the fortieth symphony.

genre/west-afrikaanse-muziektradities.text: Between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, more than twelve million Africans were shipped to the Americas as slaves, most of them from West and Central Africa. They took with them music that was unknown in Europe: rhythms in several layers at once, call and response between a lead singer and a group, music as a fixed part of work, dance and faith, and instruments from which the banjo descended. At Congo Square in New Orleans, enslaved Africans were allowed to dance, sing and drum on Sundays until well into the nineteenth century. Those elements are present in virtually all the African American music that followed.
genre/west-afrikaanse-muziektradities.listen: In this field recording of Atsiagbekor, an old war dance of the Ewe in Ghana, hear how the drums and the bell each play a pattern of their own, layered over one another, and how the group answers the lead singer.

genre/west-coast-jazz.text: In the 1950s, Cool Jazz acquired a variant of its own in California, played by musicians who also worked in the film and television studios. In 1952 in Los Angeles, Gerry Mulligan started a quartet without piano with Chet Baker, so that baritone saxophone and trumpet play in counterpoint. The quartet of Dave Brubeck from San Francisco recorded Time Out in 1959, with Take Five by the saxophonist Paul Desmond.
genre/west-coast-jazz.listen: Count along in Take Five: it is in five beats, divided into three plus two.

genre/westerse-orkestrale-en-indie-gamem.text: From 2001, Western games were given scores that could rival film. Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori opened Halo: Combat Evolved (2001) with a male choir in Gregorian style, followed by strings and rock drums. For Journey (2012), Austin Wintory wrote a score in which a solo cello follows the player and grows along with the journey; it was the first game score to receive a Grammy nomination. In The Last of Us (2013), Gustavo Santaolalla brought his sober guitar style to a game. For the indie game Celeste (2018), Lena Raine made electronic music with piano. In God of War (2018), Bear McCreary used Nordic colours and a heavy choir. In games, music often responds directly to what the player does.
genre/westerse-orkestrale-en-indie-gamem.listen: Listen to how a single instrument, such as the cello in Journey, takes on the role of the player and how the orchestra grows around that instrument.

genre/work-songs-en-field-hollers.text: On the cotton and sugar plantations of the southern United States, enslaved Africans sang while they worked. In work songs, a lead singer sings a line and the group answers, in the rhythm of the work: call and response. A field holler is the calling and singing of one person out in the fields, with a free handling of pitch. In church and at secret gatherings, the spirituals arose. After the abolition of slavery in 1865, these forms lived on, among other places in prisons and work gangs, where Alan Lomax recorded them in the twentieth century.
genre/work-songs-en-field-hollers.listen: In Po' Lazarus, hear the lead singer and the group that answers, with the blows of the axes as the rhythm.

genre/znamenny-gezang.text: When the Kievan Rus' adopted Christianity from Byzantium in 988, Greek church chants came with it. Russian singers made of them a monophonic chant of their own, named after the znamena or kryuki: hook-shaped signs that do not indicate individual notes but melodic turns that the singer knows by heart. The melodies are ordered in eight church modes. After the church reforms of Patriarch Nikon in the seventeenth century, it was above all the Old Believers who preserved this centuries-old chant.
genre/znamenny-gezang.listen: Ex Libris sings a troparion for the feast of the Trinity in the old znamenny style. All the voices sing one melody together. Where do they stretch a single syllable over a whole series of notes?

genre/zuid-afrikaanse-jazz.text: In the townships of Johannesburg and Cape Town, jazz mixed with local styles such as marabi and kwela. In 1959, the pianist Dollar Brand (later Abdullah Ibrahim), the alto saxophonist Kippie Moeketsi and the trumpeter Hugh Masekela formed The Jazz Epistles, the country's first Black bebop group with an LP of its own. After the Sharpeville massacre of 1960, the apartheid laws became stricter and many musicians left for abroad. In 1962 in Zürich, Dollar Brand met Duke Ellington, who had a record of his trio made. The Blue Notes of the pianist Chris McGregor played at the Antibes festival in 1964 and stayed in London, where the big band Brotherhood of Breath later arose. Ibrahim's Mannenberg of 1974 became a song of resistance in South Africa.
genre/zuid-afrikaanse-jazz.listen: Hear the repeated, hymn-like chord sequence that keeps running beneath the improvisations.

genre/zweedse-pop-abba.text: ABBA won the Eurovision Song Contest in April 1974 with Waterloo. Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus wrote the music together, Björn mainly the English lyrics, and the voices of Agnetha and Frida were recorded over one another several times. From the 1970s, Sweden built a hit industry of its own.
genre/zweedse-pop-abba.listen: Dancing Queen does not begin with a verse but with a piece of the chorus: the strongest moment comes straight away.

techniek/8-track.text: The aircraft builder Bill Lear designed the Stereo 8 in 1964: a cartridge with an endless loop of magnetic tape and eight tracks, four stereo programmes side by side. From the 1966 models, Ford offered the player in its cars, and for the first time you chose for yourself what you heard on the road. In the United States, the 8-track was enormously popular in the 1970s, especially in the car. Because an album was divided over four programmes, there was sometimes a click in the middle of a song, after which the song carried on. Around 1980, the compact cassette displaced the format.
techniek/8-track.listen: This is what you heard from the car speakers in the 1970s: why does this music work so well on the motorway?

techniek/ableton.text: Gerhard Behles and Robert Henke made techno in Berlin as Monolake. They wrote their own software in order to perform live with a computer. Together with Bernd Roggendorf, they developed that idea into Ableton Live, which was released in 2001. Other programs were made for the studio, Live above all for the stage. You launch separate pieces of music, loops, and they always run in time. The program also stretches recordings or compresses them until they fit the tempo. DJs and producers used it both to perform and to compose. Skrillex made his EP Bangarang in 2011 largely on tour, with Live on a laptop.
techniek/ableton.listen: Listen to the repeated snippets: how are separate loops stacked on top of one another and taken away again?

techniek/auto-tune.text: Andy Hildebrand used mathematics from the oil industry to measure the pitch of a voice. His software Auto-Tune, released in 1997, nudges flat or sharp notes imperceptibly to the right pitch. For Cher's Believe, the producers set the correction speed to zero. As a result, the voice jumped from note to note without a transition, with an audible kink. What was supposed to be inaudible became an effect. T-Pain made it his trademark, and in trap, afrobeats and hyperpop, Auto-Tune became an ordinary part of the voice.
techniek/auto-tune.listen: Listen to the long notes: does the voice glide naturally, or does it jump from note to note with a kink?

techniek/beatsampler.text: With the E-mu SP-1200 of 1987 and the Akai MPC60 of 1988, a producer could record a snippet of a record, chop it into pieces and lay those on pads. By tapping the pads, you play the pieces like a drum kit of samples, and a built-in sequencer arranges them into a pattern. Hip hop thus became a collage of drums, horns and bass lines from old records. The short sampling time and the somewhat grainy sound of the SP-1200 became a sound of their own. J Dilla played the pads in by hand, without quantize, which is why his beats swing so loosely.
techniek/beatsampler.listen: Which snippets come from old records? Can you hear the grain and the repetition of a sample?

techniek/bladmuziek.text: Before the gramophone became commonplace, you bought a song on paper. Many middle-class families had a piano in the living room and played the latest hits themselves. From the 1880s, music publishers settled in Manhattan, and by 1900 most of them were on West 28th Street. So much clattering of pianos sounded from the open windows that the street was nicknamed Tin Pan Alley, after the tin pans. Publishers employed staff songwriters and paid pianists to play new songs in shops and theatres. After the Ball by Charles K. Harris, from 1892, became one of the biggest hits.
techniek/bladmuziek.listen: These songs were sold mainly as sheet music: are they easy to sing along to and to play at home on a piano?

techniek/breakbeat.text: In 1969, on Amen, Brother by The Winstons, the drummer Gregory Coleman played a drum solo of a few seconds. Hip hop producers sampled that break in the late 1980s. In the early 1990s, producers in London went further: they sped up the Amen break and other breaks to well above 160 beats per minute and chopped them into small pieces with samplers, which they put in new orders. Beneath them, they laid heavy bass lines from dub. This is how jungle arose, and from it drum and bass.
techniek/breakbeat.listen: Do you recognise the same drum break at a different tempo? Listen to how the pieces have been cut into a new order.

techniek/cassette.text: The team of Lou Ottens at Philips in Hasselt developed a small plastic box containing magnetic tape, which was presented in 1963. Philips released the format to other manufacturers, and the cassette became a worldwide standard. From then on, anyone could record music at home, copy it and make a mixtape of their own. After the Sony Walkman of 1979, you took that music out on the street as well. Bands released their first demos on cassette, and in Algeria, raï spread mainly on cheap cassettes, outside the radio.
techniek/cassette.listen: This song spread through copies and tapes: what does the sound tell you about who it was meant for?

techniek/cd.text: Philips and Sony developed the compact disc together, and it came onto the market in 1982. Music is stored on it as digital code: 44,100 measurements per second per channel, read by a laser. A CD does not hiss and does not wear out, and holds well over an hour of music. In the 1990s, the CD became the standard and the industry earned more than ever, partly because people bought their old records again. But a digital copy is exactly identical to the original. With a CD burner and a computer, the road to free copying lay open.
techniek/cd.listen: Listen to the silences and the quiet passages: do you hear hiss or ticks, as with a record or cassette?

techniek/daw.text: In 1991, Digidesign released Pro Tools, a system with which you could record and edit multitrack audio on an Apple computer without tape. Such a program is called a digital audio workstation, or DAW. In 1999, Ricky Martin's Livin' la Vida Loca became the first number 1 hit to be recorded and mixed entirely in Pro Tools. Later, programs such as Logic, Cubase, FL Studio and Ableton Live turned every laptop into a studio. A bedroom producer can now make a complete record at home, with plug-ins that imitate old synthesizers and drum machines.
techniek/daw.listen: This song was made in the computer: can you hear how tightly edited and precise everything is, with every part in its place?

techniek/drumstel.text: Around 1900, an orchestra often had several percussionists: one for the bass drum, one for the snare drum and the cymbals. William F. Ludwig played in circus and theatre orchestras in Chicago and found the wooden pedals of his day too slow for ragtime. In 1909, he patented a pedal with a spring, which springs back by itself after every stroke. With his brother Theobald, he started a drum company. Now one musician played the bass drum with his foot and the rest with his hands. This is how the drum kit came about. Chick Webb and Gene Krupa made it, in swing, an instrument for spectacular solos.
techniek/drumstel.listen: Listen to the bass drum: can you hear the drummer's foot, and what are his hands doing at the same time?

techniek/dub.text: In Kingston, producers made an instrumental version without vocals for the B-side of singles. The engineer King Tubby went further: in his small studio, he dropped instruments in and out on the mixing desk, added long echo and reverb, and filtered the sound. In this way, a new track was made from an existing recording: dub. The mixing desk was his instrument. Ideas from dub, such as space, a heavy bass and the remix, returned in hip hop, jungle, trip hop and dubstep.
techniek/dub.listen: Notice what drops out and comes back: which instrument disappears into the echo, and when?

techniek/dx7.text: The Yamaha DX7 of 1983 did not work with filters but with FM synthesis: one wave makes the frequency of another go up and down very quickly. The principle came from John Chowning of Stanford University. The sound is clear, glassy and metallic, good for electric pianos, bells and bright basses. The DX7 was affordable and reliable and became one of the best-selling synthesizers ever. Because programming was difficult, many musicians used the factory sounds, such as the electric piano and the slap bass. These defined the sound of the 1980s.
techniek/dx7.listen: Find the clear, slightly metallic synth sound or the punchy synth bass: this is what FM sounds like.

techniek/elektrische-gitaar.text: In a big band, an acoustic guitar disappeared behind the horns. In the early 1930s, George Beauchamp and Adolph Rickenbacker in Los Angeles built a lap steel guitar with a pickup, a magnet with a coil that converts the vibration of the string into current. In 1936, Gibson released the ES-150, a hollow-body jazz guitar with such a pickup. In the band of Benny Goodman, Charlie Christian showed that the guitar could now be a solo instrument. In Chicago after the war, blues musicians such as Muddy Waters made a raw, loud city sound with it.
techniek/elektrische-gitaar.listen: The guitar is at the front: is it playing chords, or long melodic lines like a horn player?

techniek/elektrische-opname.text: Until 1925, musicians sang into a large horn, which scratched the vibrations directly into the record. Anyone who played softly did not register. Western Electric developed a system with an electric microphone and an amplifier, and the record companies Victor and Columbia took it up in 1925. From then on, recordings sounded fuller and clearer, with low notes and soft details. Singers could sing intimately close to the microphone. That way of singing is called crooning, and it became the sound of the popular music of the 1930s.
techniek/elektrische-opname.listen: The singer does not have to shout: can you hear how soft and close the voice sounds?

techniek/fairlight.text: In 1979, the Australians Peter Vogel and Kim Ryrie released the Fairlight CMI, a computer with a keyboard and a light pen. It could record a real sound digitally and place it under the keys, at any pitch: a sampler. The idea of the Mellotron now worked without tapes, with any sound you could record. The Fairlight was so expensive that only stars and big studios could afford it. Peter Gabriel, Kate Bush and the producer Trevor Horn built whole records with it.
techniek/fairlight.listen: Do you hear sounds that begin like real instruments or noises, but are repeated unnaturally exactly?

techniek/fl-studio.text: At the Ghent software company Image-Line, the nineteen-year-old Didier Dambrin wrote a simple program for making drum rhythms. In early 1998, FruityLoops was released: a grid of boxes in which you click with the mouse where a beat should fall. It grew into a complete studio and has been called FL Studio since 2003. A free trial version existed, and a generation of bedroom producers learned to make beats with it. Soulja Boy made Crank That with that trial version, the Dutchman Martin Garrix worked on Animals in it, and YoungKio built the beat of Old Town Road with it, which he sold online for a few tenners.
techniek/fl-studio.listen: These beats were made on a computer at home: can you hear the pattern that is repeated again and again?

techniek/fonograaf.text: In 1877, Thomas Edison built, in his laboratory in Menlo Park, a device that could capture and play back sound. A needle scratched the vibrations of a voice into a layer of tinfoil, later into a wax cylinder. For the first time, you could hear music without a musician standing in the room. The cylinders were hard to copy and sounded thin, but they turned a performance into something that you could keep, sell and take with you. Brass bands, popular songs and recitations were the first music to be sold in this way.
techniek/fonograaf.listen: Listen through the crackle: what is left of the music, and what is missing compared with a modern recording?

techniek/fuzz.text: During a recording by Marty Robbins in Nashville, a channel of the mixing desk broke. The guitar solo in Don't Worry, a hit in 1961, therefore sounded buzzing and distorted, and the public loved it. The sound engineer Glenn Snoddy and Revis Hobbs built a circuit that created that effect on purpose. From 1962, Gibson sold it as the Maestro FZ-1 Fuzz-Tone, one of the first effects pedals. From then on, any guitarist could choose between clean and dirty with a single footswitch. Fuzz became the sound of garage rock, psychedelia and later grunge.
techniek/fuzz.listen: Compare the fuzz sound with an ordinary amplified guitar: does it buzz, does it crackle, does it sound like a horn?

techniek/gated-reverb.text: Gated reverb means reverb with a gate. In 1979, at Townhouse Studios in London, Peter Gabriel recorded his third solo album, with Phil Collins on drums. The new mixing desk had a microphone in the recording room for talking to the musicians. It made soft sounds as loud as loud ones, and so blew up every stroke and the reverb of the room. The engineer Hugh Padgham put a gate on it that cuts the sound off abruptly. In this way, every stroke sounded enormous, followed by sudden silence. Gabriel built Intruder around that sound, and Collins used it in In the Air Tonight. It became the drum sound of the 1980s.
techniek/gated-reverb.listen: Listen to the drums: how big does a stroke sound, and how quickly is the reverb gone afterwards?

techniek/grammofoon.text: Emile Berliner recorded sound not on a cylinder but on a flat disc. The advantage: from one original, you could make thousands of copies with a press. Around 1925, 78 revolutions per minute became the usual speed. One side of such a shellac record holds about three minutes of music, and for decades that length determined how long a pop song lasts. The record turned music into a mass product. Through gramophone records, jazz and blues reached an audience that had never seen the musicians live.
techniek/grammofoon.listen: Notice the length: does the song fit into about three minutes, and can you hear that the musicians planned for it?

techniek/hammond.text: In 1935 in Chicago, Laurens Hammond built an electric organ for churches that could not afford a pipe organ. Rotating discs, tonewheels, generate the notes, and with sliders, drawbars, you mix in the overtones. Don Leslie devised a speaker cabinet with rotating horns that gives the organ a floating, undulating sound. Jimmy Smith made the Hammond a jazz instrument, and Booker T. Jones the second lead sound of soul at Stax. In British rock, it sounded solemn, as in a church, or else distorted and hard.
techniek/hammond.listen: Can you hear the floating and undulating of the organ? That is the rotating Leslie speaker.

techniek/ipod-itunes.text: In October 2001, Apple presented the iPod: a small player with a hard disk and a click wheel, with ‘a thousand songs in your pocket’. In April 2003, the iTunes Store opened, where you could legally download songs for 99 cents each. From then on, you bought a single song instead of a whole album, and the single returned as a file. Apple's adverts, with silhouettes dancing to music by bands such as Jet and Feist, became a way of making a hit in themselves.
techniek/ipod-itunes.listen: This song was heard in an iPod advert: why does it suit an image of someone dancing with earbuds?

techniek/jukebox.text: In 1927, AMI put a coin-operated machine on the market that was electrically amplified and offered a choice of ten records. In the 1930s and 1940s, such jukeboxes stood in cafés, roadside diners and bars all over America. For a few cents, the public chose for itself what was played. As a result, record companies knew exactly which songs were catching on, and from the 1940s, Billboard kept separate jukebox charts. Fast, danceable records by jump blues bands such as that of Louis Jordan were played to death in Black neighbourhoods.
techniek/jukebox.listen: Why would this song work well in a noisy café with a jukebox in the corner?

techniek/les-paul.text: In 1952, Gibson answered Fender with a solid body of its own, designed in collaboration with the guitarist and inventor Les Paul. The Les Paul is heavier than a Fender, with a carved top and later double pickups, humbuckers, which hummed less. It sustains a note for a long time and sounds full and warm. In the 1960s, British blues guitarists discovered that a Les Paul through a loudly turned-up amplifier gave a thick, singing tone. That made it the guitar of blues rock and hard rock.
techniek/les-paul.listen: Listen to how long the guitar notes hang on before they die away.

techniek/linndrum.text: In 1980, Roger Linn released the LM-1, the first drum machine with digital recordings of real drums instead of electronically imitated sounds. You programmed a pattern and the machine played it back tightly and endlessly, with a built-in option to give the rhythm a little swing. In 1982, the cheaper LinnDrum followed. The machines can be heard on countless hits of the 1980s, from The Human League and Michael Jackson to Prince, who often used the drums unusually tuned and processed.
techniek/linndrum.listen: Do the drums sound like a drummer or like a machine? Notice how identical every stroke is.

techniek/lp.text: In 1948, Columbia presented the long-playing record: a vinyl disc with finer grooves that turns at 33⅓ revolutions per minute. One side held well over twenty minutes of music instead of three. At first the LP was intended mainly for classical music, but jazz musicians used the space for long improvisations and singers such as Frank Sinatra made albums built around a single mood. In the 1960s, the album became an art form in rock: a coherent whole with a sleeve, a running order and sometimes a concept.
techniek/lp.listen: This song was made for an album: what would be lost if you heard it on its own on the radio?

techniek/magneetband.text: At the radio exhibition in Berlin in 1935, AEG showed the Magnetophon, a recorder that captured sound on a tape with a magnetic coating from BASF. After the war, the American company Ampex rebuilt the technology; the Ampex 200 came onto the market in 1948. Tape was a revolution: you could cut a recording, splice it, play it backwards and record over it again. Composers in Paris and Cologne used it to make new music from sounds and tape loops. Pop studios used tape to join together the best parts of different takes.
techniek/magneetband.listen: Here the tape itself is the instrument: which sounds come from cutting, speeding up or recording over one another?

techniek/meersporen.text: As early as around 1950, Les Paul recorded parts over one another by copying from one tape recorder to another. At Ampex, Ross Snyder devised a way to record on a second track while hearing the first in sync. In 1957, Les Paul received the first eight-track recorder. With it, a band no longer had to play all at once: every part could be recorded separately, redone and mixed later. Pop music thus became something you build in layers, with dozens of voices and instruments that were never together in one room.
techniek/meersporen.listen: Try to count the layers: how many voices and instruments do you hear that could not possibly have been played live at the same time?

techniek/mellotron.text: Beneath every key of a Mellotron is a strip of recording tape with a recording of a real instrument: a violin, a flute, a choir. If you press a key, that strip of tape runs past a playback head. After about eight seconds it runs out. The instrument was built in Birmingham from 1963, on the model of the American Chamberlin. The strings and choirs sound not quite real and float a little, and precisely that became a sound of its own. The Mellotron is a forerunner of the sampler and became the sound of prog rock.
techniek/mellotron.listen: Do the strings or choirs sound like a real orchestra? Notice how the notes float a little.

techniek/midi.text: Until 1983, synthesizers of different brands could not talk to one another. Dave Smith of Sequential and Ikutaro Kakehashi of Roland proposed a joint standard, MIDI, which was demonstrated for the first time in January 1983 at the NAMM music trade show in Anaheim. Via MIDI, instruments and computers tell one another which note is sounding, how loud and for how long. With a single keyboard, you could play several synthesizers, or have a computer play everything back. Home studios with an Atari computer and a sampler thus became affordable. Every DAW still works with MIDI.
techniek/midi.listen: Everything in this song runs tightly together: which parts might a computer be driving here?

techniek/minimoog.text: The large modular Moog was a cabinet full of cables for a studio. In 1970, the Minimoog arrived: a portable synthesizer with the most important components built in permanently, with no patch cords. You put it on a stage next to the organ, and the synthesizer became an ordinary band instrument. The Minimoog plays one note at a time and is famous for its fat bass lines and sharp lead sounds. Bernie Worrell played the bass with it in the funk of Parliament, Kraftwerk used it on Autobahn, and Gary Numan brought it into synth-pop.
techniek/minimoog.listen: Find the deep, round synthesizer bass or the bright synth melody: which of them is the Minimoog playing?

techniek/moog.text: From 1964 in Trumansburg, Robert Moog built synthesizers from separate modules that you connected with patch cords. An oscillator makes a tone, a filter removes overtones from it, an envelope determines how the tone starts and dies away. The modules control one another with electrical voltage. In 1968, with Switched-On Bach, Wendy Carlos showed what the instrument could do, and the album was an enormous success. After that, rock bands used the Moog for solos and new tone colours. The characteristic sound lies above all in the filter, which makes a tone ‘open up’.
techniek/moog.listen: Do you hear a tone that opens up from dull to bright? That is the filter of the Moog.

techniek/mp3-napster.text: At the Fraunhofer Institute in Erlangen, Karlheinz Brandenburg and his colleagues, among others, developed the MP3: a file format that leaves out what the ear barely hears. A song becomes about ten times smaller as a result. In June 1999, the student Shawn Fanning in Boston, with Sean Parker, released Napster, a program with which millions of people downloaded MP3s from one another's computers for free. Metallica and the record companies went to court, and in 2001 Napster went offline. The sharing carried on, and CD sales never recovered.
techniek/mp3-napster.listen: This song played a part in the history of the MP3 and Napster. Read the explanation and think about why this song in particular.

techniek/mtv.text: On 1 August 1981, MTV began in the United States, a television channel that broadcast music videos all day long. The first video was Video Killed the Radio Star by The Buggles. A pop star now also had to look good on screen, with clothes, hairstyle and a story. British synth-pop and New Romantic groups, who were already preoccupied with image, conquered the American charts in this way. In its first years, MTV played almost only white rock; it was only when Michael Jackson's videos reached the channel that this changed.
techniek/mtv.listen: This song became big with a music video: which images go with it in your head?

techniek/pianola.text: In 1895 in Detroit, Edwin Votey built a device that made a piano play by itself. A roll of paper with holes in it ran past a row of openings; wherever air could pass through a hole, a key went down. The Aeolian Company put the Pianola on the market in 1898. Anyone who could not play the piano could now still hear the latest ragtime at home. In the 1920s, the player piano was an ordinary piece of furniture in America, and Scott Joplin and George Gershwin played rolls themselves. Later, Conlon Nancarrow wrote music so fast and complicated that only a player piano can play it.
techniek/pianola.listen: Here it is not a pianist playing but a roll of paper: can you hear that in the rhythm or in the touch?

techniek/plaatgalm.text: Reverb is the sound that goes on floating through a hall after a note. Studios made reverb with a separate echo chamber, but such a room takes up space and always sounds the same. In 1957, the German company EMT in Lahr released the EMT 140: a thin steel plate of about one by two metres, suspended in a wooden cabinet. A driver makes the plate vibrate and pickups capture the reverb. With a damper, you make the reverb shorter or longer. At RCA Studio B in Nashville, the engineer Bill Porter used such a plate to give the voices of Roy Orbison, the Everly Brothers and Elvis Presley a clear sheen.
techniek/plaatgalm.listen: Listen to the voice at the end of a phrase: how long does it go on sounding, and does that sound like a real hall?

techniek/portastudio.text: A multitrack studio was expensive and large in the 1970s. In September 1979, TEAC showed the 144 Portastudio under the brand name TASCAM: a mixing desk and a recorder for ordinary cassettes in a single box. You could record four tracks separately and layer them, for 899 dollars. From then on, musicians made their demos at home. On 3 January 1982, Bruce Springsteen recorded songs on a Portastudio in his bedroom in Colts Neck. Those recordings appeared almost unprocessed as the record Nebraska. In the 1990s, Guided by Voices and Elliott Smith made whole records on four-track recorders. That raw home sound is called lo-fi.
techniek/portastudio.listen: Can you hear the hiss and the room? What does that home sound add to the song?

techniek/precision-bass.text: A double bass is large, quiet and awkward to transport. In 1951, Leo Fender released the Precision Bass: an electric bass guitar with frets, built as a solid body. Thanks to the frets, a bass player played ‘precisely’ in tune, hence the name. With an amplifier, the bass could finally rise above drums and guitars. In the 1960s, the bass guitar became a melodic instrument. In the Motown studio in Detroit, James Jamerson played agile, syncopated bass lines that form the heart of the hits.
techniek/precision-bass.listen: Follow only the bass: does it play one note per beat, or a melody of its own with runs?

techniek/prophet-5.text: The Minimoog could play only one note at a time. Dave Smith and John Bowen of Sequential Circuits in San Jose built a synthesizer that plays five notes at once, and therefore chords as well. That is called polyphonic. What was new above all was the memory: a small computer remembered all the settings of a sound, so that you could change sounds at the press of a button, on stage too. Smith showed the Prophet-5 in January 1978 at the NAMM show in California. It became a sound of new wave and synth-pop, from The Cars and Japan to Talking Heads, and later of Michael Jackson and Madonna.
techniek/prophet-5.listen: Listen to the keyboards: is the synthesizer playing separate melodies or full chords, and how does the sound change?

techniek/radio.text: In November 1920, the station KDKA in Pittsburgh began regular broadcasts; in The Hague, Hanso Idzerda had already been broadcasting music in 1919. In the 1920s, a radio set arrived in millions of living rooms. Music was suddenly free and could be heard everywhere at the same time. Big bands played live on the radio and in this way became known nationwide, and programmes such as the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville made country music a national genre. Anyone who got on the radio could reach a whole country in a single evening.
techniek/radio.listen: Imagine hearing this from a box in the living room: which instrument carries best over a small speaker?

techniek/rhodes.text: Harold Rhodes developed an electric piano without strings. A little hammer strikes a thin metal tine, and a pickup converts that vibration into current, as with a guitar. After a bass version from 1959, the full Fender Rhodes came onto the market in 1965. The sound is warm and softly bell-like, and growls when you play harder. In the late 1960s, Miles Davis had his pianists play the Rhodes, and the instrument became a fixture of jazz rock and soul, and later of neo-soul.
techniek/rhodes.listen: Listen to the keyboard part: can you hear the soft, bell-like sound, and the growl when it is struck hard?

techniek/ritmebox.text: In 1959, the organ manufacturer Wurlitzer released the Side Man, a cabinet with a rotating disc that triggered electronic drum sounds in the rhythm of a waltz, rumba or foxtrot. It was intended for organists in bars and restaurants, who thus did not have to pay a drummer. Later, electronic organs had such rhythms built in. In 1971, Sly Stone made a Maestro Rhythm King the basis of his record There's a Riot Goin' On. The stiff, dry rhythm suddenly sounded tired and menacing. Timmy Thomas set an organ with built-in rhythms to a bossa nova, and Shuggie Otis jammed for hours with his own drum machine.
techniek/ritmebox.listen: The rhythm comes from a machine: does it sound like a drummer, or do you hear precisely the mechanical quality of it?

techniek/saxofoon.text: The Belgian instrument maker Adolphe Sax, born in Dinant, moved to Paris in 1842. There he designed a brass wind instrument with a reed and keys, as on a clarinet. In 1846, he obtained a patent on it. The saxophone was intended for military bands: loud enough for outdoors, but more supple than a trumpet. In jazz, it became a voice that could sing, shout and whisper. Coleman Hawkins made the tenor saxophone a solo instrument, and Charlie Parker played the lightning-fast lines of bebop on it. After the war, the screaming sax gave rhythm and blues and early rock 'n' roll their power.
techniek/saxofoon.listen: Three times a saxophone: when does it sound like a singing voice, and when like a shout?

techniek/single.text: In 1949, RCA Victor answered the LP with a small vinyl record with a large hole, which turns at 45 revolutions per minute. Each side held one song of a few minutes. The single was cheap, unbreakable and fitted in jukeboxes and portable record players. That made it the product for teenagers with pocket money. In the 1950s, rock 'n' roll was above all single music: an A-side for the radio, a B-side to go with it, and a new chart every week. The form of the three-minute pop song lasted in this way.
techniek/single.listen: How quickly does the song get to the point? Count how many seconds it takes before the singing begins.

techniek/slapback-echo.text: In his small Sun studio in Memphis, Sam Phillips used two tape recorders to make a short echo: the sound was recorded and played back once more a fraction of a second later. That single quick repeat, the slapback, gave voices and guitars a spacious, bouncing sound. It became the sound of Elvis Presley's early records and of rockabilly. Shortly afterwards came stand-alone echo units with a tape loop, such as the Echoplex and the Italian Meazzi, which guitarists of Indo rock and surf often used.
techniek/slapback-echo.listen: Listen to the end of every word: can you hear the short second slap right behind the voice?

techniek/soundcloud.text: SoundCloud was founded in 2007 by the Swedes Alexander Ljung and Eric Wahlforss and made its home in Berlin. On the platform, anyone can upload their own tracks for free, and listeners can comment at an exact moment in a song. Around 2015, a new rap scene grew out of it, SoundCloud rap: young artists who recorded at home, with distorted 808s, short songs and plenty of Auto-Tune. Hyperpop also found its first audience there. A track could go viral there without a label or radio.
techniek/soundcloud.listen: Can you hear that this was made at home? Notice the distorted bass and how short and direct the song is.

techniek/soundsystem.text: In the poor districts of Kingston, from the 1950s, sound systems were in operation: mobile discotheques with home-built amplifiers and enormous speaker cabinets. At first they played American rhythm and blues, later Jamaican records of their own. Owners such as Duke Reid and Coxsone Dodd began recording records themselves in order to have something their competitor did not have. The deejay talked and toasted over the music, a forerunner of rap. DJ Kool Herc took that habit to the Bronx, where it grew into hip hop.
techniek/soundsystem.listen: The deejay talks and shouts over an existing record: can you hear how the voice becomes an instrument?

techniek/spotify.text: In October 2008, Spotify started in Stockholm. You no longer bought songs but paid for access to the whole catalogue, or listened for free with adverts. The playlist took over the role of the album, and an algorithm helps choose what you hear. A stream only counts after thirty seconds, and that changed the form of pop songs: shorter intros, the hook early, shorter songs. Artists are paid per stream. At the same time, music from Lagos or Johannesburg could reach a worldwide audience through playlists.
techniek/spotify.listen: How quickly does the hook arrive? Count the seconds until you know what the song is about.

techniek/steelgitaar.text: According to tradition, the Hawaiian schoolboy Joseph Kekuku discovered around 1889 in Honolulu that he could play a guitar by sliding a piece of metal over the strings. He laid the guitar flat on his lap. Such a lap steel plays gliding notes that sound like a sighing voice. Hawaiian musicians took the instrument on tour through America and Europe, and in the 1930s it acquired an electric pickup. In country music, it became indispensable. Later, pedals were added that change the tuning of individual strings. Bud Isaacs introduced that pedal steel in 1954 on Slowly by Webb Pierce, and ever since it has wept in almost every country song.
techniek/steelgitaar.listen: Listen to the gliding notes: does the guitar sound like an instrument, or more like a voice sighing?

techniek/steelpan.text: In Trinidad, African drums were banned at carnival in the 1880s. Revellers therefore struck bamboo sticks, and in the 1930s also tins, dustbins and car parts. In 1939, the first band to play only on metal paraded through Port of Spain. Boys such as Winston ‘Spree’ Simon discovered that a dented piece of metal gives different notes. Around 1947, Ellie Mannette and others made pans from oil drums, which lay everywhere after the war. In 1951, a steelband from Trinidad introduced the instrument in London. The steelband became the sound of carnival and calypso.
techniek/steelpan.listen: You hear only metal pans: which ones play the melody, and which the bass and the rhythm?

techniek/stereo.text: As early as 1931, the British engineer Alan Blumlein applied for a patent on a way of recording sound with two channels, so that you hear where an instrument is positioned. It only became a product after the LP. Westrex developed a groove containing two channels at once. In late 1957, the label Audio Fidelity pressed the first stereo record in New York, and in 1958 the major record companies followed. At first they were mainly demonstration records on which percussion bounced from left to right. In the 1960s, rock bands discovered the possibilities. Producers placed vocals and drums entirely to the left or right, and psychedelic bands let sounds float through the room.
techniek/stereo.listen: Listen with headphones: what do you hear on the left, what on the right, and does anything move from one side to the other?

techniek/stratocaster.text: In 1954 came the Stratocaster: a solid body with a rounded shape, three pickups and a tremolo arm with which you can make the pitch drop and spring back. By switching between the pickups, the same guitar sounds clear and glassy or warm and round. Buddy Holly made the Strat known in rock 'n' roll, Hank Marvin of The Shadows in Europe. Jimi Hendrix used the tremolo arm and feedback to make notes wail and dive. Since then, the Stratocaster has been one of the most copied guitars in the world.
techniek/stratocaster.listen: Can you hear the clear, slightly glassy sound of the guitar, and somewhere a note that bends or drops?

techniek/studio-instrument.text: In 1966, the Beatles stopped performing and began to work mainly in the studio. With the producer George Martin and EMI engineers, they used tape loops, tape played backwards, varied tape speed and ADT, a trick with which a second tape recorder automatically doubles a voice. In Los Angeles, Brian Wilson of The Beach Boys built Pet Sounds with studio musicians. A record was no longer an account of a performance, but a work that could only exist in the studio. Psychedelic rock and art rock grew out of this.
techniek/studio-instrument.listen: Which sounds on this recording could no band play live on a stage?

techniek/talkbox.text: A talk box makes a guitar talk. A loudspeaker blows the sound through a small plastic tube into the musician's mouth. The musician forms vowels with lips and tongue, and a microphone picks up the result. The idea had existed since the late 1930s, but the devices were too quiet for a rock stage. In 1973, the sound engineer Bob Heil of Marissa, Illinois, built a powerful version for Joe Walsh, who used it on Rocky Mountain Way. Peter Frampton turned it into a crowd-puller. In funk, Roger Troutman of Zapp had a synthesizer sing through the talk box, and that sound returned in G-funk.
techniek/talkbox.listen: Can you hear where the guitar stops and the voice begins? Which words or vowels can you make out?

techniek/tb-303.text: The TB-303 Bass Line was meant for guitarists who only practised and missed a bass player. The little box has one oscillator, a filter and a sequencer in which you program a bass line note by note, with accents and gliding notes. It did not sound like a bass guitar and flopped; in 1984 it went out of production. In Chicago, producers discovered that you could turn the knobs for cutoff and resonance while playing. The same bass line then squeals, squelches and wails. That sound was given the name acid.
techniek/tb-303.listen: The notes stay almost the same, but the sound keeps changing: can you hear the filter opening and closing?

techniek/technics.text: In 1972, Matsushita released the SL-1200 under the name Technics, a turntable with direct drive. The motor is strong and holds its speed even when you hold the record back or turn it backwards with your hand. DJs in the Bronx used two turntables to repeat the drum break of a funk record endlessly. By moving the record rhythmically back and forth, scratching arose, which made the turntable an instrument. The SL-1200 became the standard in hip hop and club DJ booths all over the world.
techniek/technics.listen: Can you hear the rasping scratch sound? That is a DJ moving a record back and forth by hand.

techniek/telecaster.text: The hollow-body electric guitar would howl with feedback when the amplifier was turned up loud. In Fullerton in 1950, the radio repairman Leo Fender built a guitar from a solid plank of wood, first called Esquire and Broadcaster, and from 1951 Telecaster. The neck was bolted on and the guitar was made in a factory from separate parts. As a result, it was reliable and affordable. The Telecaster sounds sharp and twangy. It became the instrument of country guitarists in Bakersfield and Nashville, and later of pub rockers and punks.
techniek/telecaster.listen: Can you hear the sharp, biting attack of the guitar, cutting through between the other instruments?

techniek/theremin.text: The Russian physicist Lev Termen built an instrument around 1920 that you play without touching it. Two antennas measure the distance to your hands: one controls the pitch, the other the volume. The sound is a gliding, singing tone that recalls a voice or a singing saw. Clara Rockmore played classical music on it. In Hollywood in the 1940s and 1950s, the theremin became the sound of suspense, madness and flying saucers. Robert Moog began building theremins in the 1950s, before he made synthesizers. Later, rock musicians such as Jimmy Page also used the theremin.
techniek/theremin.listen: The tone glides from note to note without jumps: what does that sound remind you of?

techniek/tiktok.text: TikTok, the app for short videos from the Chinese company ByteDance, broke through worldwide in 2018. Users choose a sound clip and make a video to go with it. A few seconds of a song can thus circulate millions of times, made by users themselves. Old Town Road by Lil Nas X became a worldwide hit in this way in 2019. Since then, record companies have been looking for songs with a moment that works in a short video, and artists sometimes release a snippet first to see whether it catches on.
techniek/tiktok.listen: Which part of this song would you choose for a fifteen-second video?

techniek/tr-808.text: The Roland TR-808 came onto the market in 1980 as a tool for demos. It does not use recordings of real drums: every sound is generated electronically. Musicians thought it sounded fake and Roland stopped production after a few years. Second-hand, it became cheap, and young producers discovered the bass drum that rings out long and low, a sub-bass that you feel more than hear. The 808 became the basis of electro, Miami bass and trap, and in hip hop ‘808’ now simply means: a deep, long bass.
techniek/tr-808.listen: Listen to the bass drum: is it a short thud, or a long low tone that slowly dies away?

techniek/tr-909.text: The TR-909 of 1983 was the successor to the 808. Bass drum, snare and toms are still generated electronically, but the cymbals and hi-hats are digital recordings. The machine also had MIDI. The 909, too, sold badly and became cheap second-hand. Producers in Chicago and Detroit used the solid, dry bass drum on every beat and the hissing open hi-hat in between. That pattern became the basis of house and techno, and then of almost all European dance music.
techniek/tr-909.listen: Count along with the bass drum on every beat, and listen to the hi-hat that keeps hissing in between.

techniek/transistorradio.text: The Regency TR-1 of 1954 was the first transistor radio to reach the shops. Transistors replaced the large radio valves, so that a radio fitted in your coat pocket and ran on batteries. Teenagers could now listen to their own music out of their parents' sight: on the beach, on the street, in their bedroom. Producers tuned their records to that tiny speaker. At Motown, mixes were checked on cheap speakers, and Phil Spector built a sound that sounded full even through a tiny radio.
techniek/transistorradio.listen: Play this song on a phone speaker: what holds up, and what drops away?

techniek/versterker.text: An amplifier is supposed to make a signal larger without changing it. If you turn it up further than intended, the peaks of the sound wave are clipped and the guitar sounds rough and tearing: overdrive. As early as 1958, Link Wray poked holes in his speaker to get that sound. In 1962, in his music shop in Hanwell, in west London, Jim Marshall built an amplifier that rock guitarists could make sound loud and distorted. Hard rock and heavy metal grew out of that sound, with the power chord as their foundation.
techniek/versterker.listen: Is the guitar clean or distorted? Can you hear the difference between single notes and the heavy chords?

techniek/vocoder.text: In the 1930s at Bell Labs, Homer Dudley developed the vocoder, intended to send speech efficiently over telephone lines. The device splits a voice into frequency bands and imposes their variation on another sound, a synthesizer for example. The result is a speaking machine. In the early 1970s, Wendy Carlos used the vocoder in the music of A Clockwork Orange, and Kraftwerk made the sound of the man-machine with it. In electro and Italo disco, the robot voice then sounded everywhere.
techniek/vocoder.listen: Where do you hear the robot voice? Does it sound like a singing synthesizer or a speaking machine?

techniek/wah-wah.text: In 1966 at the Thomas Organ Company, Brad Plunkett developed a pedal with a filter that you open and close with your foot. As a result, the guitar sounds as if it is saying ‘wah-wah’, like a trumpet with a mute. The pedal was sold under the brands Vox and Cry Baby. Jimi Hendrix made a talking, wailing voice of it. In funk and soul in the early 1970s, guitarists instead played the wah rhythmically, and so it became the sound of blaxploitation films such as Shaft.
techniek/wah-wah.listen: Can you hear the guitar ‘talking’? Notice how the sound opens and closes in time with the rhythm.

techniek/walkman.text: Sony's founder Masaru Ibuka wanted to listen to music on long flights. Engineers in Tokyo built a small cassette player for the purpose, without a speaker and without a record button, with lightweight headphones. On 1 July 1979, the Walkman was in the shops in Japan. Within Sony, many had doubts: who wants a cassette player that cannot record? It became a worldwide success. Music became something personal, a soundtrack to your own walk or bus ride. The city became the backdrop to your music. Young people played their home-made cassettes on it, full of new wave, post-punk and synth-pop.
techniek/walkman.listen: Imagine hearing this on headphones while you walk through the city: what does the music do to what you see?

techniek/wall-of-sound.text: At Gold Star Studios in Los Angeles, the producer Phil Spector had several guitarists, pianists and drummers play the same part at the same time, and sent the sound through an echo chamber. In this way, all the instruments melted into a single thick wall of sound, the Wall of Sound. It was made to sound overwhelming even from a small radio. Spector treated the studio not as a place to capture a band but as an instrument in itself. Girl groups such as The Ronettes were given their grand sound this way, and later Bruce Springsteen built on it.
techniek/wall-of-sound.listen: Try to pick out separate instruments. Can you, or do you mainly hear one big mass?

techniek/youtube.text: YouTube began in 2005 as a website where anyone could share videos. Within a few years it was the place to which the music video moved, and for many young people the most important way of listening to music. Artists could find an audience without a record company: Justin Bieber was discovered through videos on YouTube. Chicago drill rappers such as Chief Keef became known in 2012 with home-made clips. Gangnam Style by PSY was the first video to be watched more than a billion times, and brought K-pop to worldwide attention.
techniek/youtube.listen: This song became big through a video: what about the sound or the hook makes it suited to sharing?

werk/2-unlimited-no-limit.text: In the spring of 1993, No Limit by 2 Unlimited was at number one in more than 35 countries. The face of the group was Dutch: the rapper Ray Slijngaard and the singer Anita Doth. The music came from the Belgian producers Phil Wilde and Jean-Paul De Coster. It was the biggest international success of Dutch pop musicians in years, and the song had hardly any lyrics.
werk/2-unlimited-no-limit.listen: Count the components: synth riff, rap, chorus and break. In the British version, the rap is cut out, apart from the word techno.

werk/2pac-2pacalypse-now.text:
This debut appeared in November 1991. The recording took place at Starlight Sound Studio in Richmond, California. The production team Underground Railroad of Digital Underground made the music. The title plays on the 1979 war film Apocalypse Now.

It is a socially critical hip hop album. The lyrics deal with racism, police violence, poverty, gang violence, teenage pregnancy and drug use. Trapped, I Don't Give a Fuck and Soulja's Story stood out for their violent lyrics aimed at the police and the government. Brenda's Got a Baby became the second single. Vice President Dan Quayle called the record unfit to be released, after the lawyer of a police officer's killer had said that the album influenced his client. Critics praised the lyrics and the storytelling, but found the beats unimpressive. In 1995, the album went gold.
werk/2pac-2pacalypse-now.listen: Listen to Brenda's Got a Baby: follow the story that 2Pac tells and notice how the rap raises a social problem.

werk/2pac-me-against-the-world.text:
By late 1994, 2Pac was already a controversial rapper. He had a series of violent incidents behind him, was convicted in a sexual abuse case and received a prison sentence of one and a half to four and a half years. A day before the jury gave its verdict, he was shot and robbed in a studio in New York. Against that background, he made Me Against the World. He wanted to show the hip hop world his respect for the genre and made his lyrics more personal and thoughtful than before. The album appeared in March 1995, while he was in prison.

The producers included Shock G and Easy Mo Bee. Many songs are about fear, despair and poverty, such as If I Die 2Nite and Lord Knows. Old School is nostalgic and Dear Mama is a tribute to his mother. The album reached number 1 in the American chart and was counted by critics among the best hip hop albums. Dear Mama received a Grammy nomination.
werk/2pac-me-against-the-world.listen: Listen to Dear Mama and notice how the lyric addresses his mother. Which tone does he choose: reverent, grateful or sad as well?

werk/2pac-r-u-still-down-remember-me.text:
R U Still Down? (Remember Me) was released on 25 November 1997, well over a year after the death of 2Pac, and was his first album without his own involvement. The double album consists mainly of unreleased work from 1992 to 1994, from the time of Strictly 4 My N.I.G.G.A.Z., Thug Life: Volume 1 and Me Against the World. The title comes from handwritten track lists that he made at the time. The production was led by We Got Kidz Productions, together with Afeni Shakur and Lisa Smith-Putnam. They gave old recordings new instrumentals.

The lyrics date from the time before the rivalry between the East Coast and the West Coast. In Open Fire, Thug Style and Only Fear of Death, a premonition of his death can be heard, according to the source. Do for Love and I Wonder If Heaven Got a Ghetto became hits. Critics were divided: Entertainment Weekly found many songs hardly worthy of demo status, but saw his talent breaking through.
werk/2pac-r-u-still-down-remember-me.listen: Listen to Do for Love and notice how the soft, melodic mood of the song contrasts with the rawer songs elsewhere on this double album.
